source.subject: Biology
source.unit: Unit 1 — Diversity in the Living World
source.source_scope: Only the content printed on PDF page 9: chapter summary and the ten end-of-chapter exercises, including the displayed scientific-name and taxonomic-sequence options.

questions.question: According to the summary, what is true about the variety of plants and animals?
options: Millions have been identified and described, but many remain unknown
All plants and animals have been identified
There is little variety among organisms
questions.explanation: The summary says millions of plants and animals have been identified and described, while many remain unknown.
questions.source_text: Millions of plants and animals have been identified and described but a large number still remains unknown.

questions.question: Which kinds of variation in organisms are mentioned in the summary?
questions.explanation: The summary names size, colour, habitat, physiological features and morphological features as dimensions of organismal variety.
questions.source_text: The very range of organisms in terms of size, colour, habitat, physiological and morphological features

questions.question: The branch of knowledge dealing with identification, nomenclature and classification is called:
questions.explanation: The summary defines taxonomy as the branch dealing with these aspects.
questions.source_text: The branch of knowledge dealing with these aspects is referred to as taxonomy.

questions.question: According to the summary, taxonomic studies are useful in which areas?
questions.explanation: All four listed uses are explicitly mentioned in the summary.
questions.source_text: useful in agriculture, forestry, industry and in general for knowing our bio-resources and their diversity.

questions.question: What does the summary say about the basics of taxonomy such as identification, naming and classification?
options: They are universally evolved under international codes
They are different in every individual classroom
They do not use rules or principles
questions.explanation: The summary states that these basics are universally evolved under international codes.
questions.source_text: The basics of taxonomy like identification, naming and classification of organisms are universally evolved under international codes.

questions.question: How many words comprise the scientific/biological name described in the summary?
questions.explanation: The summary describes the binomial name as comprising two words.
questions.source_text: a correct scientific/biological name comprising two words as per the binomial system of nomenclature.

questions.question: According to the summary, organisms are identified and assigned a correct scientific name based on:
options: Only the colour of the organism
questions.explanation: The summary explicitly connects correct identification and naming with resemblances and distinct differences.
questions.source_text: Based on the resemblances and distinct differences, each organism is identified and assigned a correct scientific/biological name

questions.question: What do all taxonomic categories together constitute?
questions.explanation: The summary says all categories together form a taxonomic hierarchy.
questions.source_text: All the categories constitute a taxonomic hierarchy.

questions.question: Which question is explicitly asked in the exercise section on this page?
options: Why do all organisms have the same habitat?
Why do plants belong to Animalia?
questions.explanation: Exercise question 1 asks why living organisms are classified.
questions.source_text: Why are living organisms classified?

questions.question: Which issue about classification systems is raised in exercise question 2?
options: Why scientific names contain three words
questions.explanation: Exercise question 2 asks why classification systems change from time to time.
questions.source_text: Why are the classification systems changing every now and then?

questions.question: What does exercise question 3 ask the learner to choose?
options: Criteria to classify people they meet often
A scientific name for every person
questions.explanation: The third exercise asks what criteria one would choose to classify people met often.
questions.source_text: What different criteria would you choose to classify people that you meet often?

questions.question: Exercise question 4 asks what we learn from identification of:
questions.explanation: The exercise explicitly refers to identification of individuals and populations.
questions.source_text: What do we learn from identification of individuals and populations?

questions.question: Which mango scientific name is written correctly in exercise question 5?
questions.explanation: The exercise contrasts Mangifera Indica with Mangifera indica; the latter follows the naming rule described earlier in the chapter.
questions.source_text: Mangifera Indica; Mangifera indica

questions.question: Which task about taxon is requested in exercise question 6?
options: Define a taxon and give examples at different hierarchical levels
List only local names of plants
questions.explanation: Exercise question 6 asks for the definition of a taxon and examples at different hierarchical levels.
questions.source_text: Define a taxon. Give some examples of taxa at different hierarchical levels.

questions.question: Which option is the correct sequence among the choices printed in exercise question 7?
questions.explanation: Of the three printed choices, option (c)—Species, Genus, Order, Phylum—follows ascending order among those categories.
questions.source_text: (c) Species → Genus → Order → Phylum

questions.question: What does exercise question 8 ask learners to collect and discuss?
options: All Latin words in the chapter
questions.explanation: Exercise question 8 asks learners to collect meanings of species and discuss differences in meaning for higher plants and animals versus bacteria.
questions.source_text: Try to collect all the currently accepted meanings for the word ‘species’.

questions.question: Which terms are listed in exercise question 9 for learners to define and understand?
questions.explanation: The exercise lists phylum, class, family, order and genus.
questions.source_text: (i) Phylum (ii) Class (iii) Family (iv) Order (v) Genus

questions.question: What does exercise question 10 ask learners to illustrate?
options: Taxonomical hierarchy with suitable plant and animal examples
The life cycle of a housefly
questions.explanation: The last exercise asks learners to illustrate the hierarchy with a plant and an animal example.
questions.source_text: Illustrate the taxonomical hierarchy with suitable examples of a plant and an animal.

questions.question: Which statement best combines two points from the summary?
options: Taxonomy helps study organism diversity through identification, naming and classification
Taxonomy is only the study of habitats
Taxonomy replaces scientific names with local names
questions.explanation: The summary connects taxonomy with identification, nomenclature, classification and studying kinds and diversity of organisms.
questions.source_text: In order to facilitate the study of kinds and diversity of organisms, biologists have evolved certain rules and principles for identification, nomenclature and classification of organisms.

questions.question: According to the summary, an organism in a classification system represents or occupies a:
questions.explanation: The summary says an organism occupies a place or position in the classification system.
questions.source_text: An organism represents/occupies a place or position in the system of classification.
